title: Structural Engineer Enquiry Form: What to Ask Before You Quote
metaTitle: Structural Engineer Enquiry Form | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: What to put on a structural engineer enquiry form so you can price jobs faster: the fields to ask, what to leave out, and UK and Australian privacy basics.
geoDirectAnswer: A structural engineer enquiry form should ask for contact details, the client's role, site location, job type, project stage, drawings or photos, and timing, with optional notes. Leave out data you don't need to quote, add a short privacy note with a link to your policy, and tell people when you'll reply.
keyTakeaways: A structured fee proposal form gets you the details to price a job without rounds of emails.
Ask for role, site location, job type, project stage, files and timing; keep free text optional.
The ICO's data minimisation principle says collect only what you need, not data that might be useful later.
UK and Australian privacy guidance both point to telling people at the point of collection why you need their details.
Use the form's answers to route enquiries automatically and set clear expectations about your reply.
contentMarkdown:
Most structural engineering websites end with the same form: name, email, phone, message. Then the back-and-forth starts. Where is the property? What kind of job is it? Are there drawings? Has the builder been appointed? By the time you have enough to price the work, the client may have accepted a quote from someone who asked the right questions first. A well-designed structural engineer enquiry form fixes that. It collects what you need to prepare a fee proposal in one go, filters out jobs you don't do, and shows the client you know what you're doing. This guide covers what to ask, what not to ask, and the privacy basics for firms in Australia and the UK.

### Why the standard contact form costs you work

A blank "message" box puts the work on the client, and many clients don't know what an engineer needs. You get "Need an engineer for an extension, please call", and the job starts with a phone call or three emails before you can even estimate the fee.

A structured fee proposal request form changes that. The client answers a few specific questions, attaches what they have, and you can reply with a fee or a short list of follow-up questions. It also helps you sort enquiries: a homeowner wanting a wall removed and a developer with a multi-storey project need very different responses.

### What to ask on a structural engineer enquiry form

Keep it short enough to finish on a phone, and ask only what changes your fee or your decision to quote.

#### 1. Who the client is

- Name, email and phone
- Their role: homeowner, builder, architect or designer, developer, strata or body corporate, other

The role tells you how they'll brief you and who else is involved. An architect will usually send drawings; a homeowner may need guidance on what to provide.

#### 2. Where the site is

- Site address or suburb/town and postcode

Location affects travel time, local council or building control requirements, and whether the job is in your service area at all. If you only cover certain areas, say so next to this field.

#### 3. What the job is

A dropdown or checkboxes work better than free text here. Typical options:

- Wall removal or opening
- Extension or alteration
- New build
- Inspection or structural report (for example cracking, movement, pre-purchase)
- Retaining wall
- Remedial or repair design
- Certification or sign-off
- Civil: drainage, subdivision, driveways or similar
- Other (with a short description)

#### 4. What stage the project is at

- Just exploring
- Architectural drawings in progress
- Drawings complete, ready for engineering
- Builder appointed or works started
- Works complete, need inspection or certification

Stage tells you urgency and scope. A job where works have started and the builder is waiting is very different from early design.

#### 5. Files

- Upload drawings, plans or photos (PDF, JPG, PNG, DWG if you accept it)

For inspections, photos of cracks or defects are often very useful. Set a sensible file size limit and say what it is.

#### 6. Timing

- When do you need the engineering by?

#### 7. A short description

- Anything else we should know?

Put this last and keep it optional. By now the structured answers have covered the essentials.

### What not to ask

Extra fields can put people off finishing the form, and collecting data you don't need creates privacy obligations.

The UK's data minimisation principle is a useful test even if you're in Australia. The ICO's guidance on [data minimisation](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/) says personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for your purpose. It adds that you must not collect personal data on the off-chance that it might be useful in the future.

For an enquiry form, that usually means leaving out:

- date of birth
- full postal address of the client when you only need the site address
- budget, unless it genuinely affects whether you'll quote
- marketing preferences bundled into a required field

### Privacy notices: UK and Australia

#### UK

The ICO's guidance on the [right to be informed](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/individual-rights/right-to-be-informed/) says you must give people privacy information at the time you collect their data. That includes your purposes, lawful basis, retention period and who you share the data with, in clear and plain language. A short note under the form with a link to your full privacy notice is a practical way to do this.

#### Australia

The OAIC's guidelines on [APP 5](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-5-app-5-notification-of-the-collection-of-personal-information) explain that an APP entity collecting personal information must take reasonable steps to notify the person of certain matters, or ensure they're aware of them. These include its identity and contact details, the purposes of collection, its usual disclosures and information about its privacy policy. These steps should be taken at or before the time of collection where practicable.

For online forms, the OAIC's examples of reasonable steps include clearly and prominently displaying these matters in the form, or providing a readily accessible and prominent link to a notice. Whether the Privacy Act applies to your firm depends on your circumstances, so check the OAIC's current guidance. This isn't legal advice.

Either way, the practical step is the same: a brief, plain-English note under the form explaining why you're collecting the details and what you'll do with them, plus a link to your privacy policy.

### Example: before and after

Here's an invented example of the same enquiry coming through two different forms.

**Before (basic contact form):** "Hi, need an engineer for my house. Can you call me? – Sam"

**After (structured form):**

| Field | Answer |
|---|---|
| Role | Homeowner |
| Site | Suburb and postcode within your service area |
| Job type | Wall removal or opening |
| Stage | Architectural drawings complete |
| Files | Floor plan PDF, two photos of the wall |
| Timing | Builder starting in six weeks |
| Notes | Load-bearing wall between kitchen and dining room |

With the second version you can check the drawings and estimate the fee straight away, often without needing a call first.

### Making the form work harder

#### Route enquiries automatically

Use the job type and stage answers to send each enquiry to the right engineer, tag it in your CRM and trigger the right reply. An inspection request might get an automatic email asking for more photos, while a new build goes straight to a senior engineer. My guide to [automating lead triage into your CRM](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html) shows how.

#### Set expectations after submitting

The confirmation message and email should say what happens next and roughly when you'll reply, for example "We'll review your drawings and send a fee proposal or questions within two working days". Then stick to it.

#### Put the form where people decide

Link to it from every service page and service-area page, not just the contact page. If you're working on local visibility, my guide to [local SEO for structural engineers](/blog/local-seo-for-structural-engineers.html) covers those pages.

### Enquiry form checklist

| Field or feature | Include? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Name, email, phone | Yes | To reply |
| Client role | Yes | Shapes your response |
| Site location | Yes | Travel, local rules, service area |
| Job type (dropdown) | Yes | Fee and who handles it |
| Project stage | Yes | Urgency and scope |
| File upload | Yes | Drawings and photos speed up pricing |
| Timing | Yes | Prioritising work |
| Free-text notes | Optional | Anything the fields missed |
| Date of birth, budget | Usually no | Not needed to quote |
| Privacy note and link | Yes | UK and Australian privacy guidance |
| Clear confirmation message | Yes | Sets expectations |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for structural and civil engineering consultancies in Australia and the UK, including fee proposal forms with file uploads, routing to the right engineer, and privacy notes set up properly. You can see more about my [websites for structural engineers](/industries/structural-engineers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like fewer back-and-forth emails before you can quote, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll tell you what I'd change on your current form.

title: Fractional CFO Case Studies: How to Write Them for Your Website
metaTitle: Fractional CFO Case Studies | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to write fractional CFO case studies that win discovery calls: a simple structure, client confidentiality, and FTC rules on testimonials and results.
geoDirectAnswer: A strong fractional CFO case study describes the client by industry and stage, states the problem in plain language, explains the specific work and time frame, and reports outcomes you can back up. Get written permission for names and quotes, label illustrative examples clearly, disclose unexpected connections and don't imply one client's results are typical.
keyTakeaways: Specific case studies differentiate a fractional CFO website far more than generic service taglines.
Use the same five parts every time: client, problem, what you did, what changed and an approved quote.
Anonymized case studies are fine; presenting a made-up story as a real client is not.
The FTC says endorsements must be honest, and results must not be implied as typical without support.
Testimonials on your own website are your responsibility under the FTC's reviews and testimonials rule.
contentMarkdown:
Most fractional CFO websites say the same things: "strategic financial leadership", "scale with confidence", "CFO-level insight without the full-time cost". Founders read a dozen of these before they book a call, and the sites blur together. Fractional CFO case studies are what separate you. A specific story about a business like theirs, with a clear problem, what you did and what changed, does more than any tagline. This guide covers how to write case studies for your fractional CFO website, how to handle client confidentiality, and the US rules on testimonials and results claims you need to respect.

### Why case studies matter more than taglines

A founder hiring a fractional CFO is trusting you with their numbers, their board and often their fundraising. They want evidence that you've dealt with situations like theirs. Generic service pages can't give them that; a good case study can.

Case studies also help you get found. A page about "preparing a SaaS business for its Series A" or "fixing cash flow at a growing manufacturer" matches the specific problems owners search for, and gives AI search tools concrete material to cite. My guide to [GEO and AEO](/blog/geo-aeo-generative-engine-optimization-guide.html) explains why specific, well-structured pages perform better there.

### A simple structure that works

Keep every case study to the same five parts so readers can scan them quickly.

#### 1. The client, described the way they'd describe themselves

Industry, size or stage, and location if relevant: "a 40-person B2B software company preparing to raise", "a family-owned distributor with two warehouses". If you can't name the client, this line does the work of making the story recognizable.

#### 2. The problem in their words

What was keeping the founder up at night? Month-end close taking weeks, no reliable cash forecast, a board asking questions nobody could answer, an investor data room that didn't exist. Use the language a founder would use, not finance jargon.

#### 3. What you did

The specific work: built a 13-week cash flow forecast, rebuilt the chart of accounts, introduced monthly board packs, prepared the financial model and data room, renegotiated payment terms. Mention the time frame and how many days a month you worked with them. This shows prospects what an engagement with you actually looks like.

#### 4. What changed

Outcomes, described accurately. Faster month-end close, a forecast the board trusts, a completed raise, an exit process that ran to timetable. If you use numbers, use real ones from the engagement and be ready to back them up. See the rules below before you publish any figures.

#### 5. A quote, if the client agrees

A short, honest quote from the founder adds a human voice. Get written permission for the wording and for how they're identified.

### Confidentiality: named, anonymized or composite?

Finance work is sensitive, so many clients won't want to be named. You have three honest options:

| Approach | What it looks like | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| Named | Company name, founder name and quote, with written permission | Clients happy to be public, often after an exit or raise |
| Anonymized | "A Series A SaaS company in Austin", details changed only where they'd identify the client | Most engagements |
| Clearly labeled example | "Here's how an engagement typically runs", not presented as a real client | When you have no permissioned stories yet |

What you must not do is present a made-up story as a real client engagement. If an example is illustrative, say so.

### The US rules on testimonials and results

The FTC's rules on endorsements and reviews apply to how you present client stories and quotes on your own website.

#### Endorsements must be honest and typical results matter

The FTC's [Endorsement Guides Q&A](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/ftcs-endorsement-guides-what-people-are-asking) says endorsements must be honest and not misleading, and must reflect the honest opinion of the endorser. An endorsement can't be used to make a claim the marketer couldn't legally make directly.

The same guidance explains that if an advertiser doesn't have proof that an endorser's experience represents what people will generally achieve, an ad featuring that endorser must make clear what the generally expected results are. For a fractional CFO, that means a headline result from one standout client shouldn't be presented as what every client can expect. Add context, such as the starting point and the work involved, and avoid implying it's typical unless you can support that.

#### Disclose connections readers wouldn't expect

The Endorsement Guides Q&A also says that if there's a connection between an endorser and the business that readers wouldn't expect, and it would affect how they view the endorsement, it should be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. Its examples include an endorser who is a relative or employee, or who has been paid or given something of value. If a "client testimonial" comes from a friend, a referral partner or someone who received a discount for it, say so.

#### Testimonials on your site are your responsibility

The FTC's [Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule Q&A](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/consumer-reviews-testimonials-rule-questions-answers) says a business that puts testimonials on its own website is disseminating them, not merely hosting them, and could be liable if they're fake or false.

The FTC notes that its staff guidance isn't definitive and depends on the facts. Check the current guidance and take legal advice if you're unsure. This isn't legal advice.

### Before and after: a case study summary

Here's an invented example of the same engagement written two ways.

**Before:** "We partnered with an exciting tech company to transform their finance function and unlock growth. The results were amazing!"

**After:** "**Client:** a 35-person B2B software company preparing for its first institutional raise. **Problem:** management accounts took six weeks, and there was no forecast investors could rely on. **What we did:** two days a month for nine months; rebuilt the month-end process, introduced a rolling 13-week cash forecast and a three-statement model, and prepared the data room. **What changed:** month-end now closes within the second week, and the founder used the model and data room throughout the raise. **Note:** results depend on each business's starting point."

The second version is specific, verifiable and honest about context. It's also more persuasive.

### Where case studies should live on your site

- **A case studies index**, filterable by industry and service, linked from your main navigation.
- **One page per case study**, so each can rank for its own problem and be shared on its own.
- **Short excerpts on service pages.** Put the cash-flow case study on your cash-flow forecasting page, and the fundraising story on your fundraising support page.
- **A strong call to action at the end**: "Facing something similar? Book a 30-minute call."

For the rest of the site, my guide to [what a fractional CFO website should include](/blog/fractional-cfo-website.html) covers service pages, pricing models and contact forms.

### Case study checklist

| Item | Check |
|---|---|
| Client described by industry, size and stage | Recognizable to similar founders |
| Problem in plain language | Matches what prospects search for |
| Specific work, time frame and days per month | Shows what an engagement looks like |
| Outcomes you can back up | Accurate, with context |
| Written permission for names and quotes | Protects the client relationship |
| Illustrative examples clearly labeled | Never presented as real clients |
| Unexpected connections disclosed | FTC Endorsement Guides |
| No implied "typical" results without support | FTC Endorsement Guides |
| Own page plus excerpts on service pages | Better for search and sales |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for fractional CFO and outsourced finance firms in the US, the UK and Australia, including the Longfield Financial Advisory website in the UK. That includes case study libraries filterable by industry and service, clear service pages and booking forms. You can see more about my [websites for fractional CFO firms](/industries/fractional-cfo/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like help turning past engagements into case studies that win calls, [get in touch](/#contact).

title: Business Broker Valuation Page: Turn "What's It Worth?" Into Listings
metaTitle: Business Broker Valuation Page | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to build a business broker valuation page that brings in sellers: what to explain, calculators done safely, the form to use and US and UK ad rules.
geoDirectAnswer: A business broker valuation page should explain in plain English how businesses are valued, what drives value up and down, and exactly what the owner gets when they ask. Use a short, confidential form with revenue and profit bands, label any calculator as an indicative range, and make only claims you can back up.
keyTakeaways: A valuation page answers the question owners ask first and starts a relationship before they choose a broker.
Explain how value is worked out and what you offer, rather than promising a precise number online.
If you use a calculator, show a labeled range, explain its limits and route the owner to a person.
The FTC requires a reasonable basis for ad claims, and the CAP Code requires evidence for objective claims before publishing.
In the UK, only call a valuation free if the owner pays nothing beyond the unavoidable cost of responding.
contentMarkdown:
"What's my business worth?" is often the first question an owner has when they start thinking about selling. It may be months or years before they're ready to list. A business broker valuation page answers that question in a way that starts a relationship with you, rather than sending the owner to a free online calculator that spits out a number and forgets them. This guide covers what to put on a valuation page, whether to use a calculator, what to ask on the form, and the US and UK advertising rules that apply to claims about value.

### Why a valuation page is a seller lead source

Most owners aren't ready to talk about listing the first time they visit your site. They are, however, curious about value. A page built around that question:

- matches what they're already searching for
- gives you a reason to talk before they've chosen a broker
- lets you start a conversation months before a listing, when you can help them prepare

The goal isn't to give a precise number online. It's to explain how value is worked out, set realistic expectations and make it easy to ask you for a proper, confidential opinion.

### What to put on a business broker valuation page

#### Explain how businesses are valued, in plain English

Owners often have a number in their head that's based on revenue, a friend's sale or a headline. Explain the basics of how your firm approaches value: earnings and cash flow, how adjustments for owner's pay and one-off costs work, why recurring revenue and customer concentration matter, and how the market for that kind of business affects the price. You don't need formulas; you need to show you know what you're doing and that value depends on detail.

#### Say what drives value up and down

A short list helps owners see what to work on: clean financial records, a business that runs without the owner, diversified customers, documented processes, contracts that transfer. This makes the page useful even for owners who aren't selling yet, and it naturally leads to "talk to us about preparing your business".

#### Be clear about what you offer

Spell out what the owner gets when they ask:

- an indicative range after a short call
- a written opinion of value
- a formal valuation, and whether that's a separate paid service

Say whether there's a fee and what's included. Vague offers create suspicion.

#### Show relevant experience

Sectors and deal sizes you work with, and anonymized examples of businesses you've sold, used with permission. If you show a closed deal, describe it accurately.

#### Make the next step confidential and easy

A short form or a booking link, with a clear statement about confidentiality and who will see the information.

### Should you use an online valuation calculator?

Calculators can attract visitors and capture contact details, but they come with risks. An automated number can anchor an owner on an unrealistic figure before you've seen the books. And if the tool presents its output as more reliable than it is, you may have an advertising problem (see below).

If you use one:

- **Show a range, not a single figure.**
- **Label it clearly** as an indicative estimate based only on the figures entered, not a valuation.
- **Explain the main limitations** next to the result: it doesn't account for the quality of earnings, customer concentration, industry conditions or deal terms.
- **Route to a human.** The result should lead straight to "book a confidential call to discuss your business".

A simpler, lower-risk alternative is a short form that asks for a few figures and promises a personal response within a set time.

### What to ask on the valuation request form

Keep it short and ask only what you need for a first conversation.

| Field | Why it helps |
|---|---|
| Name, email, phone | To reply |
| Type of business and location | Sector and market matter to value |
| Approximate annual revenue (band) | Sizes the opportunity |
| Approximate profit or owner's earnings (band) | The starting point for most valuations |
| Years trading | Track record |
| Reason for asking (selling soon, planning, curious) | Sets the tone of your reply |
| Preferred contact method and time | Respects privacy and schedules |

Use bands rather than exact figures in the first step. Owners may be more comfortable sharing ranges before they know you, and you'll get the detail later.

#### Don't over-collect

The UK ICO's guidance on [data minimisation](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/) says personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for your purpose, and that you must not collect personal data on the off-chance it might be useful in the future. Even if you work only in the US, it's a sensible standard for a form that asks owners about their finances. Link to your privacy policy next to the form.

### Advertising rules: what you can claim about value

Valuation pages often make claims: "free valuation", "we get owners the best price", "our clients sell for more". These are advertising claims, and both the US and UK have rules about them.

#### United States

The FTC's [Advertising FAQs for small business](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/advertising-faqs-guide-small-business) set out the basic principles under the FTC Act: advertising must be truthful and non-deceptive, advertisers must have evidence to back up their claims, and ads cannot be unfair. The FAQ explains that before an ad runs, a company has to have a "reasonable basis" for its claims, meaning objective evidence. It also notes that statements from satisfied customers usually aren't enough to support a claim that requires objective evaluation.

So a claim like "our sellers achieve higher prices than average" needs real evidence behind it. If you can't support a comparative or numerical claim, don't make it.

#### United Kingdom

The CAP Code's section on [misleading advertising](https://www.asa.org.uk/type/non_broadcast/code_section/03.html) says marketing communications must not materially mislead. Marketers must hold documentary evidence to prove claims consumers are likely to regard as objective before publishing. The section also covers qualifications: marketing must not mislead by omitting significant limitations and qualifications, and qualifications must be presented clearly. That's directly relevant to calculator results and "free valuation" offers.

The same section has rules on the word "free": it must not be used if the consumer has to pay anything other than the unavoidable cost of responding. If your "free valuation" is only free when the owner lists with you, or carries other conditions, make that clear or don't call it free.

Both regulators' guidance depends on the facts, so check the current rules and take legal advice if you're unsure. This isn't legal advice.

### A before and after example

Here's an invented example of a valuation page headline and offer.

**Before:** "FREE instant business valuation! Find out what your business is REALLY worth in 60 seconds. We get our clients top dollar."

**After:** "What's your business worth? Get a confidential, indicative range from an experienced broker. Share a few figures and we'll call you within two working days to talk through how buyers would see your business. There's no charge for this conversation and no obligation to list. A formal written valuation is available as a separate service."

The second version sets accurate expectations, avoids unsupported claims and gives the owner a reason to talk to a person.

### Where the valuation page fits on your site

- **Link to it from your homepage** in the seller section, not just the footer.
- **Mention it on sector pages**: "Thinking about selling your HVAC business? Find out what it might be worth."
- **Send inquiries to the right broker automatically**, tagged by sector and timeline. My guide to [automating lead triage](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html) explains how.
- **Follow up with useful content** for owners who aren't ready, such as how to prepare a business for sale.

For the rest of the seller journey, see my guide to [business broker websites that win seller listings](/blog/business-broker-website.html).

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for business brokers and acquisition firms in the US and the UK, including valuation request pages, carefully labeled calculators, confidential inquiry forms and routing to the right broker. You can see more about my [websites for business brokers](/industries/business-brokers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like a valuation page that brings in seller conversations, [get in touch](/#contact).

The UK CAP Code requires documentary evidence for objective claims before publishing. Avoid comparative or numerical claims you can't support.

title: How to Recruit Care Workers Through Your Home Care Website
metaTitle: Recruit Care Workers Through Your Website | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to recruit care workers through your home care website: what a careers page needs, explaining checks, Google job listings and quick applications.
geoDirectAnswer: To recruit care workers through your website, build a careers page that states pay, mileage and travel time, explains how rotas work, lists areas and driving needs, and describes training and support. Explain pre-employment checks clearly, give each vacancy its own page with job posting markup, and keep the first application step short.
keyTakeaways: A careers page lets you answer the questions care workers use to compare agencies, such as pay, travel and rotas.
The CQC expects competence to be assessed before staff work unsupervised, so explaining induction and shadowing reassures new starters.
Employers must check right to work before employing someone, and must not discriminate based on where people are from.
Give each vacancy its own page with job posting structured data, and remove closed jobs promptly.
A short, phone-friendly first application step with a clear next step reduces drop-offs.
contentMarkdown:
If you run a domiciliary care agency, you probably spend as much time trying to recruit care workers as you do winning new clients. Job boards bring applications, but they present every agency the same way: an hourly rate, a postcode and a list of duties. Your own website is where you can show candidates why your agency is a better place to work, and where you can make applying quick and simple. This guide covers what a care agency careers page should include, how to get your vacancies into Google, and how the UK's recruitment rules for care providers should shape the way you describe the process.

### Why your website matters when you recruit care workers

Care workers compare agencies. They look at pay, mileage, how rotas work, how much travel is involved, what training they'll get and whether the agency treats staff well. Job adverts have limited space for all that. A good careers page answers those questions in full, and a candidate who has read it before applying already knows what to expect.

Your website can also bring in candidates directly. Google's [job posting documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/job-posting) explains that adding job posting structured data to your vacancy pages makes them eligible to appear in Google's job search experience, where people can filter by location and job title. A local care worker searching for "care assistant jobs" plus your town can find your vacancy without going through a job board.

### What a care agency careers page should include

#### Pay, mileage and travel, stated clearly

Be specific: hourly rate or range, how you pay for travel time and mileage, whether weekend and bank holiday rates differ, and how often you pay. Vague phrases like "competitive rates" don't help a candidate compare you with the agency down the road.

#### How rotas work

Explain how rotas are planned, how far in advance staff know their shifts, whether they can choose set areas or set clients, and how you handle short-notice changes. A predictable rota close to home can matter to candidates as much as pay.

#### Driving and areas covered

Say whether a full UK driving licence and access to a car are needed, and list the towns and areas your care workers cover. If you have walking rounds in some areas, say so; it widens your pool of applicants.

#### Training and progression

Describe your induction, shadowing before working alone, ongoing training and any support towards qualifications. The CQC's guidance on [Regulation 19](https://www.cqc.org.uk/guidance-regulation/providers/regulations-service-providers-and-managers/health-social-care-act/regulation-19) says providers should assess the competence of employees before they work unsupervised, and provide supervision until they're assessed as competent. It also says providers that employ social care support workers are expected to follow the Care Certificate standards to assess competence. Explaining this on your careers page reassures new starters, especially those new to care, that they won't be sent out alone before they're ready.

#### What the work is really like

Describe a typical day honestly: the kinds of visits, the support people need, and how you support staff when visits are difficult. Short quotes from your own care workers, used with permission, are more convincing than stock photos.

#### Who you're looking for

If you welcome people without previous care experience and train them, say so clearly. If some roles need experience or particular skills, explain which.

### Be clear about checks, without putting people off

Candidates will need to go through pre-employment checks, and it's better to explain them upfront than to surprise people later.

#### Right to work

GOV.UK's guidance on [checking a job applicant's right to work](https://www.gov.uk/check-job-applicant-right-to-work) says employers must check that an applicant is allowed to work for them in the UK before employing them. Checks can be done online using the applicant's share code, by checking original documents, or by using an identity service provider. The same page reminds employers that they must not discriminate against anyone because of where they're from.

On your careers page, a simple line works: "Before you start, we'll check your right to work in the UK. We'll tell you what documents to bring." If you can't offer visa sponsorship, say so clearly and neutrally.

#### Fit and proper checks

The CQC's Regulation 19 page explains that providers must operate robust recruitment procedures, including relevant checks, to make sure the people they employ are fit and proper, with the qualifications, competence, skills and experience needed for the role. It notes that "person employed" includes volunteers, contractors, and agency or bank staff.

The same GOV.UK right to work page, as part of its employer step-by-step guide, points employers to find out which Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) check is right for an employee, for example if they'll be working in healthcare. Tell candidates which checks you'll carry out, roughly how long they take and whether you pay for them.

This isn't legal advice. Check the current guidance from GOV.UK and the CQC when you write your recruitment process.

### Getting your vacancies into Google's job search

Google's job posting documentation lists the required properties for job posting structured data as the job title, description, date posted, hiring organisation and job location. It recommends adding salary, employment type and a closing date. A few rules matter:

- **One vacancy per page.** Google says job posting structured data must only appear on a page dedicated to a single job, not a list of vacancies.
- **Remove closed jobs promptly.** Expired jobs must be removed or marked as expired, and Google warns that not doing so may lead to a manual action.
- **Salary must be the actual salary.** Google notes that only employers can provide it, and it shouldn't be an estimate.

On WordPress, a simple "Vacancies" section with a form for your office team to add each role can generate this markup automatically.

### Make applying quick

Candidates often apply from a phone, between visits or after a shift. A long application form loses them.

- **Short first step:** name, phone number, postcode, whether they drive, and when they can start.
- **Optional CV upload** rather than a required one.
- **A clear next step:** "We'll call you within two working days to arrange a chat."
- **A privacy note** next to the form explaining how you'll use their details, with a link to your privacy notice. The ICO's guidance on the [right to be informed](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/individual-rights/right-to-be-informed/) says people must get privacy information at the time you collect their data.

Collect the full application, references and employment history at the next stage, when the candidate is engaged.

### Care agency careers page checklist

| Section | What to include | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Pay and travel | Hourly rate, mileage, travel time, enhanced rates | Candidates compare these first |
| Rotas | How shifts are planned and changed | Predictability matters to carers |
| Areas and driving | Towns covered, licence and car needs | Filters applicants and widens the pool |
| Training | Induction, shadowing, Care Certificate, progression | Reassures new starters |
| Real stories | Quotes from your own staff, with permission | More convincing than stock photos |
| Checks | Right to work, DBS, references explained | No surprises later |
| Vacancies | One page per role with job posting markup | Eligible for Google's job search |
| Application | Short, phone-friendly first step | Fewer drop-offs |
| Privacy | Note and link next to the form | UK GDPR right to be informed |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for home care and domiciliary care agencies in the UK, with careers sections that answer candidates' questions, vacancies with job posting structured data, and short, phone-friendly application forms. For the client side of your site, see my guide to [what a home care agency website should include](/blog/home-care-agency-website.html); for a deeper look at careers pages in general, see my guide to [recruiting through your own website](/blog/how-to-recruit-structural-engineers.html). You can see more about my [websites for home care agencies](/industries/home-care/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like your website to bring in more care workers, [get in touch](/#contact).

metaTitle: Lifting Equipment Certificates Online | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Put lifting equipment certificates online: what records customers need, what HSE says about keeping them, and how to build a secure portal in WooCommerce.
geoDirectAnswer: A lifting equipment certificate portal gives trade customers a secure login where every Declaration of Conformity, thorough examination report and inspection record is stored against each item's serial number. Show next due dates, send reminders, allow search and export, and keep documents read-only, since HSE says records should be protected from unauthorised alteration.
keyTakeaways: HSE says records should be kept of all thorough examinations, inspections and Declarations of Conformity for lifting equipment.
Records don't have to be paper, but users must be able to produce a written copy, and records should be protected from alteration.
Thorough examination reports include the next due date, so a portal can show status and send reminders.
Organise the portal by equipment item and serial number, with search, PDF download and register export.
WooCommerce customer accounts can be extended into a certificate portal with private document storage.
contentMarkdown:
If you supply, hire out or inspect lifting equipment, your customers ask for the same documents again and again: the Declaration of Conformity for a new sling, last year's thorough examination report for a chain block, the certificate an auditor wants to see this afternoon. Putting lifting equipment certificates online, in a secure customer area of your website, saves your office hours of searching and emailing and gives trade customers a reason to keep ordering from you. This guide covers what records customers need, what the HSE says about keeping them, and how to build a certificate portal into a WordPress or WooCommerce site.

### Why customers need their certificates quickly

Your customers carry legal duties for the lifting equipment they use. The HSE's guidance on [thorough examinations and inspections of lifting equipment](https://www.hse.gov.uk/work-equipment-machinery/thorough-examinations-lifting-equipment.htm) explains that records should be kept of all thorough examinations and inspections, and of the Declarations of Conformity for all lifting equipment and lifting accessories.

The same page says those records don't need to be kept in hard copy, but the user should be able to provide a written copy when necessary, for example when the enforcing authority asks or when equipment leaves their business through hire, use elsewhere or second-hand sale. The records should also be protected from unauthorised alteration.

When a site manager can't find a certificate, they ring you. If you can give them a login where every document is waiting, you've solved their problem and made yourself hard to replace.

### What records a certificate portal should hold

#### Declarations of Conformity

The HSE's [LOLER overview](https://www.hse.gov.uk/work-equipment-machinery/loler-overview.htm) explains that most lifting equipment and accessories must be accompanied by a Declaration of Conformity before being placed on the market or brought into use, and that the user should keep it. It may also avoid the need for an initial thorough examination before first use, where safety doesn't depend on installation or assembly.

The thorough examination page adds that this applies where the Declaration of Conformity is less than one year old and the equipment wasn't assembled on site. That makes the date on each DoC important, so show it clearly in the portal.

#### Reports of thorough examination

If you also carry out thorough examinations, the reports belong in the portal. The HSE explains that a thorough examination is a systematic and detailed examination by a competent person, who must complete a written report. That report must contain the information required by LOLER Schedule 1, including:

- the examination date
- the date the next thorough examination is due
- any defects found which are, or could become, a danger to people

The HSE notes there's no longer a defined format for the report, provided all 11 items listed in Schedule 1 are included.

#### Inspection records

Some equipment needs inspections between thorough examinations. The HSE says the need for and frequency of these should be decided through risk assessment. If you carry out inspections for customers, store those records alongside the examination reports.

### Using due dates to help customers and win repeat work

The HSE sets out the intervals for regular thorough examinations, unless an examination scheme specifies otherwise:

| Equipment | Interval |
|---|---|
| Lifting equipment and accessories used to lift people | Every 6 months |
| All lifting accessories | Every 6 months |
| All other lifting equipment | Every 12 months |

Examinations are also needed in other situations, including after assembly at each new location for equipment that needs it, and after exceptional circumstances such as damage, long periods out of use or major changes.

Because every report includes the date the next examination is due, your portal can do something useful with it:

- show each item's next due date and a clear status (current, due soon, overdue)
- send reminder emails to the customer's nominated contact before the due date
- let the customer book the next examination with one click

This turns the portal from a filing cabinet into a service tool, and it keeps your inspection diary full. The customer remains responsible for their own legal duties, so word reminders as a helpful service, not a guarantee.

### How the portal should work

#### Organised by equipment, not just by order

Customers think in terms of "the 2 tonne chain block in bay 3", not order numbers. Give each item a record with its serial or ID number, description, safe working load, location if the customer wants to record it, and every document linked to it over its life: the DoC, examination reports, inspection records and any repair notes.

#### Easy search and export

Search by serial number, equipment type, site or due date. Let customers download a single certificate as a PDF or export a register of all their equipment for an audit.

#### Multiple users per customer

Larger customers have several sites and several people who need access. Let a customer administrator add and remove their own users, and limit some users to particular sites.

#### Records that can't be changed

The HSE says records should be protected from unauthorised alteration. Make uploaded certificates read-only for customers, keep a history of every upload and replacement on your side, and never overwrite an old report when a new one arrives; add the new one alongside it.

#### Security and personal data

A portal holds business records and users' contact details, so treat it seriously: strong passwords, two-factor login for administrators, encrypted connections, regular backups and access logs. Collect only the user details you need, and link to your privacy notice from the login page.

### Building it on WordPress and WooCommerce

You don't need custom enterprise software to start. On a WordPress or WooCommerce site, a portal can be built with:

- **customer accounts**, extended from WooCommerce's existing "My Account" area, so trade customers use one login for ordering and certificates
- **an equipment record type** with fields for serial number, description, SWL, location and next due date
- **secure document storage** that only the right customer's users can access, with files served through the site rather than from public URLs
- **automatic linking** so that when you sell an item, its DoC is attached to the customer's account straight away
- **scheduled reminder emails** driven by each item's next due date

If you use inspection software already, the portal can often pull reports from it, so your engineers don't upload everything twice. My guide to [automating workflows with Make and Zapier](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html) shows the kind of connections involved.

### Certificate portal checklist

| Feature | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| One record per item with serial number | How customers actually find equipment |
| DoC, examination and inspection documents per item | Complete history in one place |
| Next due date and status for each item | Supports customers' examination schedules |
| Reminder emails before due dates | Repeat inspection work for you |
| Search, single PDF download and full register export | Quick answers for audits and enforcing authorities |
| Multiple users and site-level access | Fits larger customers |
| Read-only documents with upload history | HSE says records should be protected from alteration |
| Secure logins and private file storage | Protects customers' records and data |

### How I can help

I build WooCommerce stores and WordPress websites for lifting equipment and industrial tool suppliers, including trade accounts, certificate portals with equipment registers, private document storage and due-date reminders. For your product pages, see my guide to [selling lifting equipment online](/blog/selling-lifting-equipment-online.html). You can see more about my [websites for industrial suppliers](/industries/industrial-suppliers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If your office spends too long emailing certificates, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll show you how a portal could work for your business.

title: Engineering Project Portfolio: Present Projects That Win Work
metaTitle: Engineering Project Portfolio Guide | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to build an engineering project portfolio that wins work: page structure, filters, Google image best practice, client permission and testimonial rules.
geoDirectAnswer: An engineering project portfolio that wins work gives each project its own page with a plain headline, a facts table, the challenge, your approach, the result and labelled photos. Add filters by sector, service and location, use HTML images with descriptive alt text, get client permission, and link every project to your enquiry form.
keyTakeaways: Clients want to see similar projects and your exact role, not just a gallery of photos.
Use the same structure on every project page: headline, facts, challenge, approach, result and photos.
Google indexes images in HTML img elements, not CSS backgrounds, and uses alt text and nearby text to understand them.
Ask clients before publishing projects, addresses or drawings, and use photos you have the rights to.
In the UK, the CAP Code requires evidence that testimonials are genuine and permission to use them.
contentMarkdown: Builders, architects and developers judge an engineering consultancy by the work it has done. Your engineering project portfolio is where they look, and on most engineering websites it's either a gallery of unlabelled photos or a PDF capability statement nobody opens on a phone. A portfolio that wins work does more than show pictures. It shows the problem, what your firm did and why it mattered, organised so a busy client can find a project like theirs in seconds. This guide covers how to structure project pages, what to write, how to handle photos and client permission, and how to make your portfolio findable on Google. ### What clients look for in an engineering project portfolio A builder deciding whether to send you a job, or an architect assembling a consultant team, is usually asking: - Have they done work like mine, in size, type and location? - What exactly was their role? - Did they deal with anything difficult, such as poor ground, a tight site or a heritage building? - Are they reliable to work with? A wall of photos doesn't answer these. Short, structured project pages do. ### How to structure each project page Use the same structure for every project so readers can scan quickly. #### 1. A plain headline Describe what it is and where: "Two-storey rear extension and steel frame, Brunswick" or "Retaining wall and drainage design for a sloping residential subdivision". Avoid project code names that mean nothing to outsiders. #### 2. Project facts in a short table | Field | Example | |---|---| | Location | Suburb or town | | Sector | Residential, commercial, industrial, civil | | Client type | Homeowner, builder, architect, developer, council | | Our role | Structural design, inspection, certification, civil design | | Key elements | Steel frame, retaining wall, footings, remedial works | | Year | Year completed | #### 3. The challenge Two or three sentences on what made the job interesting or difficult: reactive clay, limited access, an existing structure in poor condition, a tight programme. #### 4. What you did Explain your approach in plain English, with enough technical detail to show competence but not so much that a builder or homeowner gives up. Mention how you worked with the architect, builder or certifier. #### 5. The result What was delivered and how it helped the client. Describe outcomes accurately. Never inflate them. #### 6. Photos and drawings Construction-stage photos, finished photos and, where the client agrees, simplified drawings. Site photos of steelwork and footings often say more to a builder than a polished finished shot. ### Organise the portfolio so people find what they need - **Filters by sector and service.** Let visitors narrow to "residential extensions" or "retaining walls" in one click. - **Location tags.** These help clients see you've worked near them, and support the area pages on your site. My guide to [local SEO for structural engineers](/blog/local-seo-for-structural-engineers.html) explains why genuine local content matters. - **Featured projects first.** Pick three to six strong, recent projects for the top of the page and your homepage. - **Links from service pages.** Your retaining wall service page should show your retaining wall projects. ### Photos: quality, speed and Google Images Project photos can bring visitors from Google Images, but only if they're set up properly. Google's [image SEO best practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images) include: - **Use standard HTML image elements.** Google finds images in the `src` attribute of `` elements and says it doesn't index CSS background images. Galleries built entirely from background images won't help you in image search. - **Write descriptive alt text.** Google calls alt text the most important attribute for image metadata. It also helps people using screen readers. "Steel portal frame for warehouse extension, Dandenong" is useful; a string of keywords is not, and Google warns that keyword stuffing in alt text can cause a site to be seen as spam. - **Use descriptive filenames.** Google says filenames give light clues about the subject, so `steel-frame-rear-extension-brunswick.jpg` is better than `IMG00023.JPG`. - **Place images near relevant text.** Google uses captions and surrounding content to understand images, which is another reason to write a proper description for each project. - **Balance quality and speed.** Google notes that sharp images are more appealing, but images are often the largest contributor to page size. Resize and compress photos, and use responsive images so phones don't download desktop-sized files. For more on keeping pages fast, see my guide to [Core Web Vitals on WordPress](/blog/achieving-99-core-web-vitals-wordpress.html). ### Permission, confidentiality and testimonials Before publishing a project, check: - **Client permission.** Some clients, especially developers and commercial owners, may not want their project, address or drawings online. Ask, and agree what can be shown. Use the suburb rather than the full address for residential work. - **Photo rights.** Use photos you took or have permission to use. If an architect or photographer took them, ask and credit them. - **Drawings.** Simplified or partial drawings are often enough to show your work without giving away detail the client would prefer to keep private. If you add a client quote, UK firms should note the CAP Code rules on [testimonials](https://www.asa.org.uk/type/non_broadcast/code_section/03.html). Marketers must hold documentary evidence that a testimonial is genuine and hold contact details for the person who gave it, and must not feature a testimonial without permission. Australian firms should apply the same standard: genuine quotes, used with permission. This isn't legal advice. ### Before and after: a project summary Here's an invented example of the same project written two ways. **Before:** "Residential project, Brunswick. [Six unlabelled photos]" **After:** "**Rear extension with steel portal frame, Brunswick.** A builder asked us to design a steel frame for a two-storey rear extension on a narrow terrace block, with limited crane access and an existing party wall in poor condition. We designed a lightweight steel frame that could be lifted in sections by hand, with new footings set away from the party wall, and inspected the steel before the slab pour. **Our role:** structural design and inspection. **Completed:** 2026." The second version tells a builder exactly what you did, shows you can handle awkward sites, and gives Google real text to understand the page and its photos. ### Portfolio checklist | Item | Why it matters | |---|---| | Plain headline with project type and location | Clients recognise similar work | | Project facts table | Quick scanning | | Challenge, approach and result | Shows competence, not just pictures | | Filters by sector, service and location | Visitors find relevant work fast | | Links from service and area pages | Portfolio supports every enquiry route | | HTML images with descriptive alt text and filenames | Eligible for Google Images, more accessible | | Compressed, responsive photos | Fast on site managers' phones | | Client permission and photo rights | Protects relationships | | Genuine, permitted testimonials | CAP Code rules in the UK | | Enquiry link on every project | Turns interest into fee requests | End every project page with a link to your fee proposal form. My guide to the [structural engineer enquiry form](/blog/structural-engineer-enquiry-form.html) covers what that form should ask. ### How I can help I build WordPress websites for structural and civil engineering consultancies in Australia and the UK, including filterable project portfolios with properly optimised images, service and area pages, and enquiry forms built for fee proposals. You can see more about my [websites for structural engineers](/industries/structural-engineers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html). If your best projects are hidden in a PDF, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll show you how they could work harder for you.

faq.answer: A page for each project with a plain headline, a facts table covering location, sector, client type, your role and key elements, a short description of the challenge, your approach and the result, plus labelled photos and, with permission, simplified drawings. Add filters by sector, service and location and link each project to your enquiry form.

faq.question: How can engineering project photos rank in Google Images?
faq.answer: Google's image guidance says to use standard HTML img elements rather than CSS backgrounds, write descriptive alt text without keyword stuffing, use descriptive filenames, place images near relevant text and captions, and keep images fast with compression and responsive sizes. A proper written description on each project page helps Google understand the photos.

faq.question: Do I need client permission to show a project on my website?
faq.answer: It's good practice to ask, especially for commercial and development work where clients may not want projects, addresses or drawings online. Agree what can be shown, use the suburb rather than a full residential address, and only use photos you took or have permission to use, crediting the photographer where appropriate.

faq.question: Can engineering firms use client testimonials in their portfolio?
faq.answer: Yes, if they're genuine and permitted. In the UK, the CAP Code says marketers must hold documentary evidence that a testimonial is genuine, hold contact details for the person who gave it, and not use a testimonial without permission. Firms elsewhere should apply the same standard. Check current guidance if unsure.

title: Fractional CFO Pricing Page: How to Show Fees on Your Website
metaTitle: Fractional CFO Pricing Page | Hamid Ali Asad

geoDirectAnswer: A fractional CFO pricing page should explain how you charge, show honest starting prices, ranges or at least your model, list what each level includes, state minimum terms and notice, and explain what affects the fee. Make 'from' prices genuinely available, state VAT status next to prices in the UK, and end with a clear route to a tailored proposal.
keyTakeaways: A pricing page helps founders check budget, model and commitment before booking a call.
You can show starting prices, ranges by tier or just your model, as long as what you publish is accurate.
The CAP Code says 'from' prices must not mislead by exaggerating what clients are likely to get.
VAT-exclusive prices in the UK must be accompanied by a prominent statement of the VAT payable.
The FTC treats price as a material claim, so published figures should reflect what clients actually pay.
contentMarkdown:
Should a fractional CFO firm publish its prices? Founders who land on your site often want a rough idea of cost before they book a call. Others worry that publishing prices invites price-shopping or undersells complex work. A good fractional CFO pricing page sits in between: it explains how you charge, gives honest starting points or ranges, and makes it easy to get a proper quote. This guide covers how to structure the page, how to present retainers, onboarding and project work, and the UK and US advertising rules that apply to prices and "from" claims.

### Why a pricing page helps even if you don't publish exact fees

A founder comparing fractional CFOs usually wants to know three things before talking to anyone:

- Is this in my budget, roughly?
- How does the arrangement work: monthly, by the day, by project?
- What am I committing to, and can I stop?

If your site answers none of these, you rely on the prospect booking a call just to find out whether you're affordable. A pricing page that answers them filters out poor fits and gives good-fit prospects the confidence to get in touch.

### Ways to present fractional CFO pricing

| Approach | What it looks like | Works well when |
|---|---|---|
| Starting prices | "Monthly support from £X" | You have a typical entry-level engagement |
| Ranges by tier | Two or three packages with a monthly range each | Clients fall into recognisable stages |
| Model only | Explain retainers, days and projects, no figures | Every engagement is genuinely bespoke |
| Calculator or estimator | Prospect answers a few questions for an indicative range | You have enough engagements to estimate reliably |

There's no single right answer. What matters is that whatever you publish is accurate and clearly qualified.

### What to include on the page

#### How you charge

Explain your model in plain English. Typical structures include a monthly retainer for ongoing support, a set number of days per month, a fixed-fee onboarding or diagnostic phase, and separately priced projects such as fundraising support or a finance system implementation. Say which you use and why.

#### What each level includes

If you use tiers, describe them by the client's situation rather than abstract names: "early-stage, pre-revenue", "growing, preparing to raise", "established, board reporting". For each, list what's included, such as forecasting, management accounts review, board packs, investor updates and days or hours per month, and what isn't.

#### Commitment and terms

State the minimum term, notice period and how you handle changes in scope. Founders worry about being locked in, so clarity here builds trust.

#### What affects the price

List the main factors: transaction volume, number of entities, the state of the books at the start, reporting requirements and how much hands-on bookkeeping or system work is needed. This explains why your figures are ranges and prepares prospects for the scoping conversation.

#### A clear next step

End with a short form or booking link: "Tell us about your business and we'll send a tailored proposal." My guide to [what a fractional CFO website should include](/blog/fractional-cfo-website.html) covers the enquiry form in more detail.

### The rules on prices and "from" claims

Prices on your website are advertising claims. Both the UK and the US have rules that apply.

#### United Kingdom

The CAP Code's section on [misleading advertising](https://www.asa.org.uk/type/non_broadcast/code_section/03.html) includes rules on prices. Price statements must not mislead by omission, undue emphasis or distortion. Price claims such as "up to" and "from" must not mislead by exaggerating the availability or amount of benefits likely to be obtained.

So if you advertise "from £1,500 a month", that price should be genuinely available for the service described, not a stripped-down package almost nobody buys.

The same section deals with VAT. Quoted prices must include non-optional taxes, but VAT-exclusive prices may be given if everyone the price is clearly addressed to pays no VAT or can recover it. In that case the price must be accompanied by a prominent statement of the amount or rate of VAT payable. Not every client will be VAT-registered or able to recover VAT, so if you quote prices excluding VAT, say so clearly next to the figure.

The section also says marketing must not mislead by omitting significant limitations and qualifications, and qualifications must be presented clearly. If a starting price assumes a minimum term or excludes onboarding, say so near the price, not in small print elsewhere.

#### United States

The FTC's [Advertising FAQs for small business](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/advertising-faqs-guide-small-business) explain that under the FTC Act, advertising must be truthful and non-deceptive and advertisers must have evidence to back up their claims. The FAQ lists price among the examples of claims that are "material", meaning important to a consumer's decision. Starting prices and ranges should reflect what clients actually pay.

These rules depend on the facts, so check the current guidance and take legal advice if you're unsure. This isn't legal advice.

### Before and after: a pricing section

Here's an invented example of a pricing section written two ways.

**Before:** "Affordable CFO services from just £499! Contact us for a quote."

**After:** "**How we charge.** Most clients start with a fixed-fee 60-day diagnostic, then move to a monthly retainer. **Typical monthly retainers:** £2,000–£3,500 for early-stage businesses (two days a month), £3,500–£6,000 for businesses preparing to raise (three to four days a month). Fundraising support and system projects are priced separately. **Terms:** three-month minimum, then one month's notice. **All prices exclude VAT at the standard rate.** We'll confirm your fee in a written proposal after a short scoping call."

The second version is specific, explains what drives the price and makes the qualifications clear. The figures here are illustrative only; use your own.

### Common pricing page mistakes

- **A teaser price nobody pays.** A very low "from" figure might attract clicks, but it erodes trust on the first call and can fall foul of the CAP Code rule on "from" prices.
- **Hiding the pricing page.** If founders have to dig for it, many won't. Link to it from your main navigation and from each service page.
- **Jargon-heavy package names.** "Growth Accelerator Plus" tells a founder nothing. Describe each level by the business stage it suits and what's included.
- **No mention of what's extra.** If fundraising support, system implementations or additional days are charged separately, say so on the page.
- **Out-of-date figures.** Review your prices and terms whenever your fees change, and note the date you last updated them.

### Pricing page checklist

| Item | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Plain explanation of how you charge | Answers the first question founders have |
| Starting prices, ranges or a clear model | Filters out poor fits early |
| What's included and excluded per level | Avoids disappointment later |
| Minimum term and notice period | Reduces fear of lock-in |
| Factors that affect price | Explains why fees vary |
| "From" prices genuinely available | CAP Code rule on "from" claims |
| VAT status stated next to prices (UK) | CAP Code rule on VAT-exclusive prices |
| Qualifications near the price, not hidden | CAP Code rules on qualifications |
| Clear next step to a tailored proposal | Turns interest into calls |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for fractional CFO and outsourced finance firms in the UK, the US and Australia, including the Longfield Financial Advisory website in the UK. That includes pricing and service pages written clearly, proposal request forms and booking flows. For proof to sit alongside your pricing, see my guide to [writing fractional CFO case studies](/blog/fractional-cfo-case-studies.html). You can see more about my [websites for fractional CFO firms](/industries/fractional-cfo/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like a pricing page that brings in better-fit enquiries, [get in touch](/#contact).

title: Business Broker Email Marketing: Stay in Touch With Future Sellers

metaDescription: Business broker email marketing that nurtures future sellers: building a list from your website, what to send, and the CAN-SPAM rules emails must follow.
geoDirectAnswer: Business broker email marketing keeps you in touch with owners who aren't ready to sell. Offer a specific resource such as a sale-preparation checklist, place sign-up forms on valuation and seller pages, keep seller and buyer lists separate, send short, useful emails on a regular schedule, and follow CAN-SPAM rules on headers, addresses and opt-outs.
keyTakeaways: Many owners who visit a broker's site aren't ready to sell, so email keeps you in touch until they are.
A specific offer, such as a sale-preparation checklist, gives future sellers a reason to subscribe.
Keep buyer and seller lists separate so each group gets only relevant emails.

contentMarkdown:
Most business owners who visit a broker's website aren't ready to sell. They're curious, planning a few years ahead or waiting for the right moment. If your site's only offer is "list your business with us", they leave and you never hear from them again. Business broker email marketing fixes that. A short, useful newsletter keeps you in front of future sellers until they're ready, so that when the time comes, you're the broker they already know and trust. This guide covers how to build an email list from your website, what to send, and the US rules your emails must follow.

### Why email suits business brokers

A business sale is a long, considered decision. An owner might read your valuation page today and not pick up the phone for another year or two. In between, they'll talk to their accountant, read about exit planning and possibly hear from other brokers.

Email lets you stay in touch through that whole period without being pushy. A monthly or quarterly note with something genuinely useful, such as how to prepare a business for sale or what buyers in their sector look for, keeps your name in front of them and shows you know your market.

### Building the list from your website

#### Offer something worth subscribing for

"Subscribe to our newsletter" gives an owner little reason to sign up. Offer something specific that a future seller wants:

- a checklist for preparing a business for sale
- a short guide to how buyers value businesses in their sector
- a periodic market update for their industry or region
- an exit planning timeline for owners one to three years from selling

#### Put sign-up forms where future sellers are

- on your valuation page, as an alternative for owners not ready to talk
- at the end of every article aimed at sellers
- on sector pages, offering sector-specific updates
- on your "selling your business" page

My guide to [business broker valuation pages](/blog/business-broker-valuation-page.html) covers how to turn "What's my business worth?" visitors into conversations; email gives you a way to keep the rest.

#### Ask for very little

An email address, a first name and, optionally, the type of business is enough. Extra fields can put people off, and they add to the data you're responsible for. The UK ICO's guidance on [data minimisation](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/) is a useful standard wherever you are: collect what you need for your purpose, not information that might be useful someday.

#### Explain what they're signing up for

Say what you'll send and how often: "A short email once a month with practical advice for owners thinking about selling. Unsubscribe any time." Link to your privacy policy. The ICO's guidance on the [right to be informed](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/individual-rights/right-to-be-informed/) says people should get privacy information at the time you collect their data, which a short note under the form does.

### What to send future sellers

Keep emails short, practical and focused on the owner, not on your listings. A simple mix:

| Content | Example | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| Preparation tips | "Five things buyers check in your financials" | Helps owners and shows expertise |
| Market notes | What's happening in deals in their sector or region | Keeps them informed |
| Answers to common questions | "How long does selling a business usually take at our firm?" | Builds trust |
| Recently sold examples | Anonymized deals, used with permission | Proof you close deals |
| A gentle next step | "Want a confidential chat about timing?" | Opens the door without pressure |

Send on a predictable schedule. Monthly or quarterly are both reasonable; pick what you can sustain. Consistency matters more than frequency.

### Separate your buyer and seller lists

Buyers and sellers want different things. Buyers want new listings and deal alerts; owners thinking of selling want preparation advice. Use separate lists or tags from the start so each group only gets relevant emails. Sending listing alerts to owners, or exit planning advice to buyers, is a quick way to lose subscribers.

### The US rules: CAN-SPAM

The FTC's [CAN-SPAM Act compliance guide](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business) explains that the law covers all commercial email, defined as messages whose primary purpose is the commercial advertisement or promotion of a commercial product or service. The FTC is clear that the law makes no exception for business-to-business email.

The guide's main requirements include:

- **Accurate header information.** "From", "To", "Reply-To" and routing information must be accurate and identify who sent the message.
- **No deceptive subject lines.** The subject must accurately reflect the content.
- **Identify the message as an ad.** You have leeway in how you do this, but it must be clear and conspicuous.
- **Include your postal address.** A valid physical postal address, a registered P.O. box or a registered private mailbox.
- **Explain how to opt out.** A clear, easy way to stop marketing emails, such as an unsubscribe link.
- **Honor opt-outs promptly.** Opt-out requests must be honored within 10 business days, and you can't charge a fee or ask for more than an email address to do so. Once someone opts out, you can't sell or transfer their address.
- **You're responsible for your provider.** Hiring an email marketing company doesn't transfer your legal responsibility.

The FTC says each separate email in violation can be subject to penalties of up to $53,088, so it's worth getting right. Many email platforms add an unsubscribe link and address footer for you, but check your templates.

**UK brokers:** the UK has its own rules on electronic marketing, covered in the ICO's direct marketing guidance. Check the current ICO guidance before emailing UK contacts. None of this is legal advice.

### Before and after: a newsletter email

Here's an invented example.

**Before:** Subject: "HOT NEW LISTINGS!!!" Body: a list of eight businesses for sale, sent to everyone who ever filled in a form.

**After:** Subject: "Three things buyers check first in a services business". Body: three short, practical points, a link to a longer article, one anonymized recently-sold example used with permission, and a closing line: "Thinking about timing? Reply to this email for a confidential chat." Footer with your postal address and an unsubscribe link. Sent only to the owners list.

The second email is accurate, useful and clearly from a real firm, and it follows CAN-SPAM's basics.

### Email checklist for business brokers

| Item | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Specific sign-up offer for future sellers | More subscribers than a generic newsletter |
| Forms on valuation, sector and seller pages | Captures owners who aren't ready yet |
| Minimal fields and a privacy note | Less friction, clear expectations |
| Separate buyer and seller lists | Relevant emails, fewer unsubscribes |
| Regular, useful content | Keeps you in mind until they're ready |
| Accurate sender and subject line | CAN-SPAM requirement |
| Postal address and unsubscribe link | CAN-SPAM requirement |
| Opt-outs honored within 10 business days | CAN-SPAM requirement |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for business brokers and acquisition firms in the US and the UK, including seller-focused sign-up offers, forms connected to your email platform and CRM, and separate buyer and seller journeys. For the wider seller journey, see my guide to [business broker websites that win seller listings](/blog/business-broker-website.html), and for connecting forms to your CRM, my guide to [automating lead triage](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html). You can see more about my [websites for business brokers](/industries/business-brokers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like your website to keep future sellers in touch, [get in touch](/#contact).
