title: Local SEO for Home Care Agencies: Get Found by Families Nearby
metaTitle: Local SEO for Home Care Agencies | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Local SEO for home care agencies: set up Google Business Profile as a service-area business, get reviews within UK rules and build area pages that rank.
geoDirectAnswer: Local SEO for home care agencies starts with a Google Business Profile set up as a service-area business, using your real name, a realistic service area and few categories. Ask families for reviews without incentives, follow CMA guidance if you publish reviews, and back the profile with genuine area pages and your CQC rating on your website.
keyTakeaways: Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and prominence, and better rankings can't be bought.
Domiciliary care agencies are service-area businesses and should hide the address if clients don't visit the office.
Your profile name must be your real business name; adding keywords can get it suspended.
Google prohibits incentives for reviews, and the CMA expects businesses publishing reviews to have a fake reviews policy.
Genuine area pages and a correctly displayed CQC rating support your local visibility and win families' trust.
contentMarkdown:
When a family needs home care, they usually start with a search like "home care near me" or "carers in [town]". The agencies that appear in Google's map results and the first few listings get the calls. Local SEO for home care agencies is about making sure yours is one of them, with a Google Business Profile that follows the rules, reviews that build trust, and a website that backs it all up. This guide covers what Google says about local rankings, how to set up a profile for a domiciliary care agency, how to handle reviews under UK rules, and what your website needs to support it. It's written for agencies in England.

### How Google decides which agencies appear

Google's guide to [improving your local ranking](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en-GB) says local results are mainly based on three things:

- **Relevance:** how well your Business Profile matches what someone searched for. Complete, detailed business information helps.
- **Distance:** how far each business is from the person searching, or the location they searched for.
- **Prominence:** how well known your business is. Google says this is also based on information such as how many websites link to you and how many reviews you have, and that more reviews and positive ratings can help.

The same page says there's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking. You earn it.

### Setting up your Google Business Profile as a home care agency

Google's [guidelines for representing your business](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177?hl=en-GB) cover a few points that matter for domiciliary care.

#### Your agency is a service-area business

Your carers visit people in their own homes. Google says service-area businesses should have one profile for the central office with a designated service area. If clients don't visit your office, Google says you should hide your address. If they do visit during staffed hours, you can show the address and still set a service area.

Google also says a service area generally shouldn't extend further than about two hours' driving time from where you're based. In practice, set it to the towns and postcodes you genuinely cover.

#### Branches

Google says that if you have different locations with separate service areas and separate staff at each, you can have a profile for each location. A virtual office isn't eligible, and a co-working desk only counts if it has signage, receives customers and is staffed during opening hours.

#### Use your real name

Your profile name must match your real-world business name, as used on your signage, website and stationery. Google says adding unnecessary information, such as service or location keywords, isn't permitted and could get your profile suspended. For example, "[Agency name] Home Care" is fine; "[Agency name] Home Care – Best Carers in [Town] 24/7" is not.

#### Categories, hours and contact details

Choose the fewest categories that describe your core business; Google asks for categories that complete the sentence "this business IS a…". Add your office hours, a local phone number you control and your website. If you offer an out-of-hours line, mention it in your description and on your website.

### Reviews: ask every family, within the rules

Reviews feed directly into prominence, and families read them closely.

Google's [tips to get more reviews](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122?hl=en-GB) say you can ask customers to leave reviews using a Google link or QR code, and encourage replying to reviews. The same page says offering incentives, such as discounts, in exchange for reviews, or to change or remove negative ones, is fake engagement and strictly prohibited.

UK consumer law adds its own expectations. The CMA's [short guide for businesses publishing consumer reviews](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fake-reviews/short-guide-for-businesses-publishing-consumer-reviews-and-complying-with-consumer-protection-law) says traders who publish reviews, including on their own website, should have a published policy that prohibits fake reviews and sets out their approach to incentivised reviews, and must take reasonable and proportionate steps to prevent and remove banned content. If you show reviews on your site, follow this guidance.

Practical approach for a care agency:

- Ask families for feedback at natural points, such as a care review or after the first few weeks of a new package.
- Make it easy with a link or QR code, and accept that not everyone will want to post publicly.
- Reply to every review briefly and professionally. Never share personal or care details in a reply.
- Respond to negative reviews calmly and offer to talk privately.

### What your website needs to support local SEO

Your Business Profile gets you into the map results; your website backs it up and turns the visit into a call.

#### Pages for the areas you cover

Create a page for each main town or area you serve, with genuine local detail: the villages and postcodes covered, how far ahead you can usually start a package there, and the local team. Avoid copying the same page and swapping the town name.

#### Your CQC rating, displayed correctly

If your service has a CQC rating, you must display it on your website. The CQC's guidance on [displaying ratings for community-based adult social care](https://www.cqc.org.uk/cqc-ratings-and-promotional-graphics/how-providers-must-display-ratings/community-based-adult-social-care) says to show your current rating on every website you operate that describes your services, on a permanent page that is conspicuous, clear about which service it relates to and reachable from your main navigation, such as your homepage or appropriate landing pages. It's also one of the first things a family looks for.

#### Consistent details

Use the same business name, phone number and service areas on your website as on your Business Profile, so families and Google see a consistent picture.

#### Easy contact on mobile

Many families will find you on a phone. Make the phone number large and clickable, show office hours, and keep the enquiry form short.

My guide to [what a home care agency website should include](/blog/home-care-agency-website.html) covers the full site, and my guide to [recruiting care workers through your website](/blog/recruit-care-workers-home-care-website.html) covers the careers side.

### Local SEO checklist for home care agencies

| Area | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Business Profile type | Service-area business, address hidden if clients don't visit | Google's guidelines |
| Service area | Towns and postcodes you genuinely cover | Accurate, within Google's guidance |
| Business name | Real name only, no keywords | Keyword-stuffed names risk suspension |
| Categories | Fewest that describe your core service | Relevance |
| Branches | One profile per staffed location | Google's guidelines |
| Reviews | Ask with a link or QR code, no incentives | Prominence, Google and CMA rules |
| Review replies | Brief, professional, no personal details | Trust and privacy |
| Area pages | Genuine local detail for each main area | Relevance on your website |
| CQC rating | Displayed on homepage or main landing pages | CQC requirement |
| Consistent details | Same name, phone and areas everywhere | Clear signals to families and Google |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for home care and domiciliary care agencies in the UK, with genuine area pages, your CQC rating displayed correctly, clear contact options on mobile and the technical and local SEO set up properly. You can see more about my [websites for home care agencies](/industries/home-care/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like more families to find you locally, [get in touch](/#contact).

Set a realistic service area, hide your address if clients don't visit, and build reviews. Google says local results depend on relevance, distance and prominence.

faq.answer: Google's guidelines say service-area businesses that serve customers at their locations should hide their address if customers don't visit. Avoid near-identical pages with only the town name changed, and link each page from your main navigation.

title: WooCommerce Trade Accounts for Industrial Suppliers
metaTitle: WooCommerce Trade Accounts | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to set up WooCommerce trade accounts for industrial suppliers: approval, account pricing, ex-VAT display, pay on account, UK invoice and terms rules.
geoDirectAnswer: WooCommerce trade accounts let approved business customers log in, see their own prices excluding VAT, pay on account and reorder quickly. For UK industrial suppliers, include an application and approval step, customer group pricing, clear ex-VAT labelling, compliant invoices, agreed payment terms with reminders, quick reorder, quote baskets and multi-user access.
keyTakeaways: Trade customers expect account prices, ex-VAT figures, payment on terms and fast reordering.
An application and approval step lets you run credit checks before trade prices and terms appear.
The CAP Code allows VAT-exclusive prices only for audiences who don't pay or can recover VAT, with a prominent VAT statement.
GOV.UK lists what invoices must include, and VAT invoices are needed when both businesses are VAT registered.
If no payment date is agreed, payment is late 30 days after the invoice or delivery, whichever is later.
contentMarkdown:
Most of your best customers don't buy like retail shoppers. They're contractors, maintenance teams and procurement departments who expect account prices, VAT-exclusive figures, payment on terms and a quick way to reorder the same items. Out of the box, WooCommerce is set up for customers who pay by card at checkout, so trade orders often still come in by phone and email. WooCommerce trade accounts close that gap: approved business customers log in, see their prices and order online on the terms you've agreed. This guide covers what a trade account setup should include for an industrial or lifting equipment supplier, the UK rules on invoices, VAT pricing and payment terms that shape it, and how to roll it out.

### What trade customers expect from your website

Trade buyers mostly want the website to make their job quicker:

- **Their prices, not list prices**, as soon as they log in
- **VAT shown the way they work**, usually excluding VAT with the VAT clearly stated
- **Payment on account** rather than a card at every order
- **Fast reordering** of consumables and repeat items
- **Order history, invoices and documents** in one place
- **Multiple users** for different sites or staff, with someone controlling who can order

If your website can't do these things, the website ends up as a catalogue and the real ordering happens elsewhere.

### The core features of a trade account setup

#### Application and approval

Add a trade account application form that collects the company name, company number, VAT number, delivery and invoice addresses, accounts contact and the credit you're being asked for. New applications should wait for your approval before trade prices or payment terms appear. Approval lets you run your normal credit checks before you extend terms.

#### Account-specific pricing

Set prices by customer group, such as trade, contract or distributor, or agree pricing for individual key accounts. Quantity breaks suit consumables like shackles, slings and fixings. Logged-out visitors can still see list prices, or a "log in for trade prices" prompt, depending on your strategy.

#### VAT display

The CAP Code's rules on [misleading advertising](https://www.asa.org.uk/type/non_broadcast/code_section/03.html) say quoted prices must normally include non-optional taxes. VAT-exclusive prices may be given if everyone the price is clearly addressed to pays no VAT or can recover it, and they must be accompanied by a prominent statement of the amount or rate of VAT payable.

In practice, show VAT-exclusive prices to logged-in trade customers with a clear "ex VAT" label and the VAT rate, and think carefully before showing ex-VAT prices to the general public on pages consumers can reach.

#### Payment on account

Let approved customers check out with "pay on account" up to a credit limit you set, with their purchase order number captured at checkout. Card payment can stay available for new or cash customers.

#### Invoices that meet the rules

GOV.UK's guidance on [what invoices must include](https://www.gov.uk/invoicing-and-taking-payment-from-customers/invoices-what-they-must-include) lists a unique identification number, your company name, address and contact details, the customer's company name and address, a clear description of what you're charging for, the supply date, the invoice date, the amounts charged, the VAT amount if applicable and the total owed. Limited companies must include the full company name as it appears on the certificate of incorporation. The same page says you must use VAT invoices if both you and your customer are VAT registered.

Whether invoices come from WooCommerce or your accounting system, make sure the template covers these, and that customers can download them from their account.

#### Payment terms and late payment

GOV.UK's guidance on [late commercial payments](https://www.gov.uk/late-commercial-payments-interest-debt-recovery) explains that if you agree a payment date, it must usually be within 60 days for business transactions; a longer period can be agreed if it's fair to both businesses. If no payment date is agreed, the law says payment is late 30 days after the customer gets the invoice or you deliver the goods, whichever is later. The guidance also explains that you can claim interest and debt recovery costs on late commercial payments.

Show each customer's agreed terms in their account, print them on invoices, and send automatic reminders before invoices fall due. This isn't legal or financial advice; check the current guidance and your own terms.

#### Quick reorder and quotes

Give trade customers a "buy again" list from previous orders, a quick-order form where they can enter product codes and quantities, and a quote basket for larger or custom orders such as made-to-length slings or lifting beams.

#### Users, sites and documents

Let a customer administrator add colleagues, set who can order and who can only view, and assign users to sites. Keep order history, invoices and equipment documents together. If you supply lifting equipment, this is where your certificate portal fits; see my guide to [putting lifting equipment certificates online](/blog/lifting-equipment-certificates-online.html).

### Trade account feature checklist

| Feature | What it does | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Application form and approval | Collects company, VAT and credit details; you approve | Control over who gets terms |
| Customer group pricing | Trade, contract or account-specific prices | Matches how you already price |
| Quantity breaks | Lower unit price at higher quantities | Suits consumables |
| Ex-VAT display with VAT rate | Clear labelling for trade users | CAP Code rule on VAT-exclusive prices |
| Pay on account with PO number | Checkout without a card, up to a limit | How trade customers pay |
| Compliant invoices | All items GOV.UK lists | Legal invoice requirements |
| Terms and reminders | Agreed terms shown, reminders before due | Fewer late payments |
| Quick reorder and quote basket | Repeat orders and custom requests | Saves trade buyers time |
| Users, sites and permissions | Customer controls who orders | Fits larger customers |
| Documents in the account | Invoices and certificates in one place | Fewer calls to your office |

### Common trade account mistakes

- **Approving accounts automatically.** If trade prices and payment terms switch on the moment someone registers, you lose the chance to check who they are.
- **Mixing ex-VAT and inc-VAT prices without labels.** Customers comparing a basket with a quote get confused, and consumers may see prices that don't include VAT. Label every price clearly.
- **Hiding the agreed terms.** If the customer can't see their credit limit and payment terms in their account, expect more calls to your accounts team.
- **Leaving phone orders as the default.** Without a reason to log in, such as quick reorder or downloadable invoices and certificates, customers carry on phoning.

### How to roll it out

1. **Start with your best accounts.** Invite your top trade customers first, load their pricing and terms, and ask for feedback.
2. **Connect your accounting system.** Sync customers, prices, orders and invoices so you don't key orders in twice.
3. **Move phone and email orders online gradually.** When a regular customer calls, offer to set up their login and show them quick reorder.
4. **Keep product pages strong.** Trade buyers still need specifications, safe working loads and documents on every product; see my guide to [selling lifting equipment online](/blog/selling-lifting-equipment-online.html).
5. **Watch performance.** Account pricing and large catalogues add load to WooCommerce; my guide to [scaling WooCommerce](/blog/scaling-woocommerce-hpos-caching-checkout-optimization.html) covers the technical side.

### How I can help

I build WooCommerce stores for lifting equipment and industrial tool suppliers, including trade account applications and approval, customer group pricing, ex-VAT display, pay on account, quick reorder, quote baskets and certificate portals, connected to your accounting system where possible. You can see more about my [websites for industrial suppliers](/industries/industrial-suppliers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If your trade customers still order by phone and email, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll show you how trade accounts could work for your business.

Agreed business payment dates must usually be within 60 days, though a longer period can be agreed if fair to both. You can claim interest and recovery costs on late payments.

title: Service Area Pages for Engineers: Rank Locally Without Doorways
metaTitle: Service Area Pages for Engineers | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to write service area pages for engineers that rank locally: what Google's doorway and keyword stuffing policies say, what to include, and how to link.
geoDirectAnswer: Service area pages for engineers should each give genuine local value: real projects in that area, local conditions and common job types, the approvals context, the local team and lead times, and a link to your fee proposal form. Build pages only for core areas, group smaller places regionally, link them through a hub page and avoid city-list paragraphs.
keyTakeaways: Google's spam policies treat near-identical city pages that funnel users to one page as doorway abuse.
Google lists blocks of text naming cities you want to rank for as an example of keyword stuffing.
Each area page needs genuine local content, ideally real projects you've completed there.
Start with a few core areas and group smaller suburbs or towns into regional pages.
Link area pages through a hub and to services and projects, forming a clear, browseable hierarchy.
contentMarkdown:
Most structural and civil engineering consultancies serve a patch of suburbs or towns, and most clients search with a place name: "structural engineer Footscray", "civil engineer Reading". Service area pages for engineers are how you show up for those searches. Done well, each page gives a builder or homeowner real reasons to trust you in their area. Done badly, with the same text copied twenty times and the suburb name swapped, they look like spam to Google and to readers. This guide covers what Google's policies say, what a good engineering area page contains, how many to build and how to link them.

### What Google says about location pages

Google's [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) describe "doorway abuse" as sites or pages created to rank for specific, similar search queries that lead users to intermediate pages that aren't as useful as the final destination. The examples Google lists include:

- having multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page
- creating substantially similar pages that are closer to search results than a clearly defined, browseable hierarchy

The same page describes "scaled content abuse": many pages generated mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help users, typically unoriginal content with little value, however it's created, including with AI tools.

It also lists "keyword stuffing", and one of Google's own examples is blocks of text that list cities and regions a web page is trying to rank for. The long "we serve Suburb A, Suburb B, Suburb C…" paragraph at the bottom of many engineering websites is exactly that.

None of this means area pages are banned. It means each one has to be genuinely useful to someone in that area.

### What a good engineering area page contains

Think of each area page as a short local briefing for a builder, architect or homeowner there.

#### Local work you've actually done

The strongest content is real projects in or near that area, with client permission: "Steel frame for a rear extension in [suburb]", "Retaining wall design on a sloping block in [town]". Link each one to its full project page. My guide to [engineering project portfolios](/blog/engineering-project-portfolio-website.html) covers how to write those.

#### Local conditions and common jobs

Explain what's typical in that area from an engineering point of view, based on your own experience: the housing stock, the kinds of renovations you see, site access issues, slopes, or ground conditions you commonly design for. Keep it factual and specific to your work there. If you don't have genuine local knowledge of an area, that's a sign it shouldn't have its own page yet.

#### The local approvals context

Name the council, building control body or certifiers you commonly work with in that area, and explain in general terms how your documents fit into their process. Check details with the authority rather than stating requirements from memory.

#### Practical details

Who covers that area from your team, typical lead times for inspections there, and whether you charge travel for outlying parts of it.

#### A clear next step

Link to your fee proposal form with the area pre-selected if you can. My guide to the [structural engineer enquiry form](/blog/structural-engineer-enquiry-form.html) covers what that form should ask.

### How many area pages should you build?

Fewer, better pages beat dozens of thin ones. A practical approach:

1. **Start with your core areas**, the three to eight places where you do the most work and have real projects to show.
2. **Group smaller suburbs or villages** into a regional page, such as "Inner West" or "North Somerset", instead of a page each.
3. **Add a new page only when you have something specific to say**: projects, local conditions or a local team member.

Your Google Business Profile should reflect the same reality. Google's [guidelines for representing your business](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177?hl=en-GB) say service-area businesses should set a designated service area, and that the overall service area generally shouldn't extend further than about two hours' driving time from where you're based. Keep your website's area pages consistent with that.

### Linking area pages together

Google's spam policy contrasts doorway pages with "a clearly defined, browseable hierarchy". Build that hierarchy on purpose:

- **An "Areas we cover" hub page**, linked from your main navigation or footer, listing each area page with a one-line summary.
- **Each area page links to relevant service pages**, such as inspections, extensions or retaining walls, and to local projects.
- **Each project page links back to its area page.**
- **Neighbouring areas link to each other** where it helps a reader, not as a block of links at the bottom.

### Before and after: an area page opening

Here's an invented example of the same page written two ways.

**Before:** "We are the leading structural engineers in [Suburb]. Our [Suburb] structural engineers provide structural engineering services to [Suburb] and surrounding areas including [list of 30 suburbs]."

**After:** "We've designed extensions, wall removals and retaining walls across [Suburb] for builders and homeowners for several years. Many homes here are older weatherboard houses on narrow blocks, so most of our local work involves opening up internal walls and designing new footings beside existing ones. Recent local projects include a two-storey rear extension and a retaining wall on a sloping corner block (see below). Inspections in [Suburb] are usually booked within a week."

The second version is specific, readable and only possible for a firm that really works there, which is exactly what Google and clients are looking for. Replace every detail with your own; don't copy these claims.

### Common area page mistakes

- **Swapping the suburb name in a template.** If the only difference between two pages is the place name, they're the "substantially similar pages" Google describes.
- **Generating pages in bulk with AI.** Google's scaled content policy applies however the content is created, so dozens of generated pages with no real local detail are a risk.
- **Pages for places you rarely work.** If you can't name a project or a local issue, the page has nothing useful to say. Cover those places on a regional page instead.
- **Orphaned pages.** Area pages that aren't linked from your hub, services or projects are hard for visitors and Google to find.
- **Inconsistent service areas.** If your website covers places your Business Profile doesn't, or the reverse, tidy one or the other.

### Area page checklist

| Item | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Real local projects, with permission | Proof you work there |
| Local conditions and common job types | Useful, unique content |
| Local approvals context, checked | Shows familiarity with the process |
| Team, lead times and travel notes | Practical information clients want |
| Link to fee proposal form | Turns visits into enquiries |
| Only core areas get their own page | Avoids thin, near-duplicate pages |
| Regional pages for smaller places | Covers more ground without doorways |
| Hub page and clear internal links | Browseable hierarchy, not doorway pages |
| No city-list paragraphs | Google lists them as keyword stuffing |
| Consistent with your Business Profile | Same service area everywhere |

For the wider local picture, including your Business Profile and reviews, see my guide to [local SEO for structural engineers](/blog/local-seo-for-structural-engineers.html).

faq.question: Are location pages bad for SEO?
faq.answer: Not in themselves. Google's spam policies target doorway abuse, such as many substantially similar pages for different cities that funnel users to one page, and scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings. Location pages with genuine local content, such as real projects and local conditions, are useful to readers and fit within Google's guidance.

faq.question: How many service area pages should an engineering firm have?
faq.answer: Only as many as you can fill with genuine local content. Start with the three to eight areas where you do most of your work and have projects to show, group smaller suburbs or villages into regional pages, and add new pages only when you have something specific to say about an area.

faq.question: Should I list all the suburbs I serve on my website?
faq.answer: Avoid long paragraphs listing suburbs or towns. Google's spam policies give blocks of text listing cities and regions a page is trying to rank for as an example of keyword stuffing. Instead, create a hub page linking to your core area pages and set your service area in your Google Business Profile.

faq.question: What should an engineering service area page include?
faq.answer: Real local projects shared with client permission, the typical local conditions and job types you handle there, the local approvals context, who covers the area and typical lead times, any travel charges, links to relevant service and project pages, and a clear link to your fee proposal form.
